column6: The commentary recalls quail among Israel's provision before warning of wrath; Numbers describes the wind bringing quail into the camp, supplying the wilderness scene behind that recollection.
The commentary sets provision beside wrath coming upon people; here the Lord strikes while meat is still between their teeth, making that sequence explicit.
The commentary recalls Moses returning angry after the calf; Exodus depicts him seeing the calf and breaking the tablets in anger at the foot of the mountain.
The commentary links the calf episode with wrath upon the people; God tells Moses that his anger burns against Israel and threatens their destruction.
The commentary places wrath beside forgiveness; after Moses pleads for Israel, Exodus says the Lord relented from the threatened disaster.
The commentary presents Moses returning from the calf in anger and grief; Deuteronomy says he feared the Lord's anger and recounts that the Lord listened to his plea.
The commentary connects the calf with threatened wrath; Deuteronomy says the Lord was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him and that Moses prayed for him too.
The commentary names manna and quail as gifts preceding the warning; this retelling says Israel ate and was filled after God brought the birds.
The commentary sets the bestowed food against wrath; this wilderness retelling says God's anger rose against the well-fed people and struck them.
The commentary recalls Moses' angry return after the calf; the psalm retells Israel making and worshiping a calf at Horeb.
The commentary sets wrath alongside forgiveness; this retelling says Moses stood before God in the breach to turn away destruction from the people.
The commentary says God reminds Israel of manna and quail; Exodus describes quail at evening and manna with the morning dew.
The commentary recalls provision followed by a warning against transgression; Moses says manna humbled and tested Israel, with God intending good for them at the end.
The commentary identifies manna and quail as the gifts recalled before wrath; the psalm's exodus praise names both quail and heaven's bread as God's response to Israel's request.
The commentary sets divine pleasure against wrath; this psalm contrasts a moment of divine anger with a lifetime of favor, giving that opposition a temporal shape.
The commentary says favor leaves a softened, cooled face; the priestly blessing asks God to make his face shine on the recipient, joining divine favor to a visible face.
The commentary reads the favored group as bearing a softened face; the blessing asks God to lift his countenance upon Israel and give peace, making face and favorable outcome a single formula.
The commentary joins the favored group to a shared path and visible faces; the psalm calls blessed the people who walk in the light of God's countenance.
The commentary says bestowed favor is visible in the face; this prayer asks God to bless the people and make his face shine upon them.
The commentary links bestowed favor with the path of those guided; this psalm asks that God's way and saving power become known among the nations after the face-shining blessing.
The commentary contrasts faces marked by favor with faces marked by disgrace; here those who look to the Lord become radiant and are not ashamed.
The commentary says the face bears the outcome of favor or wrath; this psalm sets the Lord's face against evildoers, giving the contrary face-image an explicit judgment setting.
The commentary connects anger with a scowling face; God asks Cain why he is angry and why his face has fallen, an unusually close bodily scene.

column5: anger at the door and choice
column6: The commentary makes the angry face part of a moral division; God tells Cain that sin crouches at the door and that he must rule over it, turning the fallen-face scene toward a choice of conduct.

The commentary contrasts an angry, fallen face with favor; Onkelos interprets God's answer to Cain in terms of forgiveness if he does well, making the face scene a question of repentance and restored standing.

column5: light of eyes refreshes the heart
column6: The commentary says favor cools and settles the eye; Proverbs says light to the eyes gladdens the heart and good news refreshes the bones, a specific bodily image of restored well-being.
The commentary describes anger as a scowling face and favor as softness; Ecclesiastes says wisdom brightens a person's face and changes its severity.
The commentary contrasts the face marked by wrath with the softened face of favor; Proverbs says a king's bright face means life and his favor is like a spring rain cloud.

column5: wrath and favor as bodily weather
column6: The commentary's contrast is between anger's harsh face and bestowed good; Proverbs compares a king's anger to a lion's growl and his favor to dew on grass.
The commentary contrasts wrath with favor and reads both on the face; Isaiah describes a moment of anger in which God hid his face, set against enduring compassion.
The commentary ends with two groups on different paths; this psalm contrasts the way of the righteous, watched by the Lord, with the way of the wicked, which perishes.

column5: life and death set before Israel
column6: The commentary distinguishes two groups by the path they take; Moses sets life and good against death and evil before Israel, framing the division as a consequential choice.
The commentary presents a path shared by those receiving favor; Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses and urges Israel to choose life, including life for their descendants.
The commentary sets the path of the favored against those who go astray; Proverbs depicts the righteous path growing brighter while the next verse gives the wicked's way as darkness.
The commentary's two groups take divergent paths; Proverbs says the way of the wicked is darkness and that they do not know what makes them stumble.
The commentary calls the way of the favored a path walked together; the psalm's shepherd restores the speaker and leads him in paths of righteousness, with goodness and mercy following.
The commentary asks for guidance onto the straight path; this psalm says God guides the humble in justice and teaches them his way.
The commentary's ن ع م family includes favor and softness; the psalm asks that the Lord's נֹעַם be upon the people and their work, a Hebrew cognate used for divine favor or pleasantness.
The commentary links the ن ع م family with good and praise; Proverbs uses Hebrew נעם for wisdom's pleasant ways and says all her paths are peace, joining the cognate to a favored way.
The commentary describes the blessed as companions on one path; the psalm calls brothers dwelling together good and נעם, using a Hebrew cognate for the pleasant quality of fellowship.
The commentary describes the favored as walking a path together; Moses urges Israel to love God, cling to him, and live, tying fidelity to a continuing way of life.
The commentary places two groups under the judgment of the day; Daniel describes some awakening to everlasting life and others to shame and everlasting contempt.
The commentary says the day's outcome appears on faces; Daniel says the wise and those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the brightness of the sky and stars.
The commentary divides the guided from those under wrath; Malachi says the day will make the distinction between the righteous who serve God and the wicked who do not.
The commentary calls the day the bearer of wrath and recompense; Malachi describes the coming day as an oven that consumes the arrogant and evildoers.

column5: healing sun for those who fear God
column6: The commentary contrasts a wrath-marked face with a softened, favored one; Malachi sets the coming day against a sun of righteousness with healing for those who fear God.
The commentary says the day carries both wrath and deliverance; Amos warns those expecting the Lord's day that it will be darkness rather than light, a direct reversal of presumed favor.
The commentary identifies the day as carrying wrath; Zephaniah calls the Lord's day a day of wrath, distress, ruin, darkness, and gloom.
The commentary makes the day the time when the two outcomes are borne; Ecclesiastes says God will bring every deed, including what is hidden, into judgment.
The commentary sets wrath against favor; after the calf episode God proclaims himself compassionate and slow to anger, framing the same episode with mercy.

The commentary holds forgiveness beside the wrath that falls on others; the covenant proclamation says God forgives iniquity while also addressing wrongdoing, refusing to collapse mercy into impunity.

The commentary pairs divine wrath with the possibility of forgiveness; after Israel refuses to enter the land, Moses appeals to God's patience and forgiveness using the attributes revealed after the calf.
The commentary contrasts the one upon whom wrath falls with those forgiven; after Moses' plea over Israel's rebellion, God answers that he has forgiven according to Moses' word.
The commentary pairs wrath with favor; the psalm describes God as compassionate, slow to anger, and abundant in steadfast love.
The commentary contrasts wrath with pardon; the psalm says God will not always accuse or keep anger forever.

column5: slow anger toward a spared city
column6: The commentary says some receive wrath while others are forgiven; Jonah objects that God is gracious and slow to anger after Nineveh is spared, making mercy to an outside city the point of his complaint.
The commentary says others are forgiven rather than struck by wrath; God answers Jonah by naming the many people in Nineveh for whom he has compassion.
The commentary says favor softens and cools the eye; Ezra describes a brief gift of divine favor that brightens the community's eyes and revives them in captivity.

column5: forgive a neighbor and be forgiven
column6: The commentary opposes wrath to favor and pardon; Sirach says a person who forgives a neighbor's wrong can seek forgiveness for their own sins, linking restraint of anger with receiving mercy.
The commentary makes wrath a consequential state; Sirach asks the angry person to remember death and the commandments, then relinquish enmity.

The commentary sets wrath and forgiveness together in the calf story; this rabbinic reading of God's revelation to Moses makes reciting the mercy attributes a liturgical route to forgiveness after Israel sins.
The commentary contrasts divine favor with wrath; this Talmudic prayer asks that God's mercy prevail over his anger, giving the contrast a Jewish devotional formulation.
The commentary distinguishes two groups by the path they follow; the Community Rule describes opposing spirits that direct human conduct and lead to different outcomes at God's visitation.

column5: light, peace, and life of truth
column6: The commentary's favored group walks a guided way and bears a softened face; the Community Rule associates the spirit of truth with enlightenment, peace, and life, giving a Jewish sectarian account of the favorable path.
The commentary distinguishes those receiving favor from those under wrath at the day; the Son of Man invites those at his right hand as blessed by the Father into the prepared kingdom.

column5: cursed ones depart from the judge
column6: The commentary uses a passive label for those upon whom wrath has fallen; here the king explicitly addresses the cursed and sends them away, making the judge's agency overt.
The commentary's day carries two opposite outcomes; Matthew closes the judgment scene with punishment for one group and eternal life for the other.
The commentary's phrase describes people with wrath upon them; John says God's wrath remains on the one who disobeys the Son, alongside the alternative of eternal life.
The commentary names the day that bears wrath and recompense; Paul calls it a day of wrath and the revelation of God's righteous judgment.

column5: glory, honor, and life for the patient
column6: The commentary contrasts wrath with the outcome of the guided; Paul sets eternal life and glory for those who persevere in doing good against the day of judgment.

column5: wrath for those who reject truth
column6: The commentary distinguishes the wrath-struck from the guided; Paul describes wrath and fury for those who reject truth and follow unrighteousness.
The commentary sets two groups under judgment; Paul names glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, Jew first and Greek as well.

The commentary contrasts a granted blessing with wrath falling on another group; Paul speaks of vessels of wrath and God's patience toward them, a close but not identical account of agency and judgment.

column5: vessels of mercy prepared for glory
column6: The commentary contrasts the wrath-struck with those granted favor; Paul pairs vessels of wrath with vessels of mercy prepared for glory, making the two-group contrast explicit.
The commentary reads Israel's food and transgression as a warning; Paul tells the church that these events became examples so they would not desire evil as Israel did.
The commentary connects Israel's rebellion with wrath; Paul warns the congregation not to grumble as the wilderness generation did, whose people were destroyed.

column5: Israel's story written for later readers
column6: The commentary uses Israel's provision and punishment to frame the path of the present reader; Paul explicitly says these events were written as instruction for those upon whom the ends of the ages have come.
The commentary recalls the calf and Moses' anger; Stephen recounts Israel making the calf and offering sacrifice to the work of their hands.
The commentary links the calf with divine wrath; Stephen interprets Israel's idolatry as the point at which God turned away and gave them over to heavenly worship.
The commentary ends with those who lose the path and those guided; Hebrews quotes God's complaint that the wilderness generation always goes astray in heart and has not known his ways.

column5: God's anger with the wilderness generation
column6: The commentary says wrath comes upon a group after rebellion; Hebrews asks with whom God was angry for forty years and answers with those who sinned.
The commentary ties the day and the path to each group's end; Hebrews says the disobedient were barred by oath from entering God's rest.
The commentary's lost group does not reach the guided path's end; Hebrews concludes that the wilderness generation could not enter because of unbelief.
The commentary describes favor as softening the face and lighting its surface; Zechariah's song says God's mercy brings a dawn from on high to visit the people.

column5: light guides feet into peace's way
column6: The commentary joins visible favor to a shared path; Zechariah says the dawn shines on those in darkness and guides their feet into the way of peace.
The commentary contrasts the faces of two groups on the day; Jesus says the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom after the wicked are removed.

column5: faces hidden from the enthroned one
column6: The commentary reads the face as bearing the mark of wrath; Revelation's rulers and people ask to be hidden from the face of the enthroned one and from the Lamb's anger.
The commentary calls the day the bearer of judgment; Revelation's terrified speakers ask who can stand when the great day of divine and Lamb's wrath has arrived.
The commentary describes the favored as a community on one path; Revelation shows an uncountable multitude from every nation standing together before the throne and the Lamb.

column5: the Lamb guides to living springs
column6: The commentary says the favored are guided on a path and their faces show the outcome; Revelation's Lamb shepherds the multitude, guides them to springs of living water, and wipes away every tear.
The commentary names prophets, truth-affirmers, martyrs, and the righteous as companions; Hebrews gathers faithful exemplars who were commended but had not yet received what was promised.
The commentary describes the favored as companions on one path; Hebrews says the earlier faithful are not made complete apart from the later community, extending the company across generations.

column5: cloud of witnesses and shared race
column6: The commentary calls the favored a group walking together; Hebrews pictures a cloud of witnesses surrounding the hearers as they run the race set before them.
The commentary says favor and judgment are visible on faces; Paul describes people with unveiled faces being transformed as they behold the Lord's glory.
The commentary links blessing with a radiant face; Paul locates the knowledge of God's glory in the face of Jesus Christ.
The commentary describes benefaction as coming upon the favored; James says every good and perfect gift comes down from above from the Father of lights.

column5: human anger does not make justice
column6: The commentary opposes wrath to favor and the straight way; James says human anger does not produce God's righteousness, an ethical warning about anger's outcome.
The commentary says favor makes the face soft while anger makes it sullen; Proverbs says a glad heart makes the face cheerful, while sorrow breaks the spirit.
The commentary says provision can precede wrath; the psalm says God granted the people's request but sent a wasting disease with it, complicating the meaning of a bestowed gift.
The commentary contrasts the two outcomes as marks borne upon a group; Moses' song says God will hide his face from a faithless generation, making withdrawal of favor a visible relational judgment.
The commentary describes wrath as a bodily heat that descends; Moses' song pictures God's anger kindling a fire that reaches the depths and consumes the land.

column5: Hebrew נעם in a pleasant inheritance
column6: The commentary associates ن ع م with good and benefaction; the psalm calls the speaker's allotted inheritance pleasant, using Hebrew נעם for the quality of a received portion.

column5: anger and wrath ruin the way
column6: The commentary divides people by the path they take; Proverbs-like instruction in this psalm says to abandon anger and wrath because they lead toward evil.
The commentary opposes a softened face to anger's scowl; Proverbs says a soft answer turns wrath away while a harsh word stirs it up.
The commentary says benefaction cools the eye and recalls food given in the wilderness; Jonathan eats honey and his eyes brighten, a concrete bodily sign of refreshment after nourishment.
The commentary contrasts wrath with forgiveness; the psalm says God has not dealt with people according to their sins or repaid them according to their iniquities.

column5: Jonah's anger at a spared plant
column6: The commentary connects anger with a bodily state and with whether wrath falls; Jonah becomes angry over the plant, while God uses that response to challenge his anger at Nineveh's rescue.
The commentary sets the wilderness provision beside wrath and pardon; Nehemiah's communal confession recalls Israel's rebellion and God's readiness to forgive, slow anger, and steadfast love.
The commentary says some receive punishment and others forgiveness; Nehemiah recounts that when Israel again did evil, God handed them over and later rescued them when they cried out.

The commentary starts the wrath scene by recalling Israel's rescue from an enemy; the psalm says God brought his people out with joy and singing, supplying the deliverance that precedes wilderness testing.

column5: the two ways of life and death
column6: The commentary closes by distinguishing groups through the path they follow; the Didache opens its teaching with the way of life and the way of death and their sharply different outcomes.

column5: two ways of light and darkness
column6: The commentary contrasts a guided way with a path of straying; Barnabas introduces two ways, one of light and one of darkness, extending that moral division in early Christian instruction.
The commentary names a group defined by straying; Barnabas details the way of darkness through its destructive practices, making the wrong path concrete.

The commentary recalls favored people falling in worship and weeping; Luke depicts a woman weeping at Jesus' feet, wetting and wiping them, an embodied act of grief and devotion that Jesus receives in a forgiveness scene.
The commentary links the favored with prostration and weeping; Hebrews describes Jesus offering prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears, tying bodily humility to being heard.
The commentary contrasts those upon whom wrath falls with the forgiven; Paul says those justified by Christ's blood will be saved from wrath through him.
